title: A House Built for Four
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 38 of 40
content:
We decided to rebuild the house because the kitchen floor sank two inches.

Toph noticed first.

Obviously.

She walked in one morning, stopped, and said, “That’s new.”

I looked around.

“What?”

“The southeast corner dropped.”

Katara froze with a kettle in her hand.

Aang looked down.

“I don’t see anything.”

Toph turned toward him. “Thank you, Eyes.”

The storm had undermined part of the old foundation. Repairs were possible, but once engineers opened the floor they found three generations of creative decisions hidden beneath it.

A beam resting on bricks.

A pipe routed through a support wall.

A previous owner had apparently used a decorative statue as structural material.

I stared into the hole.

“Can we move?”

Toph grinned.

“No.”

She loved the disaster.

The repair became a renovation.

The renovation became an argument about everything we had learned since moving in.

Aang still wanted roof access.

Toph wanted more direct foundation contact.

Katara wanted water storage integrated into the house rather than hauling clinic and household supplies in jars.

I wanted my office moved away from the kitchen because everybody treated “walking past the door” as a reason to ask me one quick question.

“There are no quick questions,” I said.

Sokka, who had invited himself into the design process, nodded solemnly.

“Only poorly scoped ones.”

I pointed at him. “Exactly.”

Toph groaned. “Two of them.”

The rebuilt house took six months.

We lived in three rooms above the academy during construction.

This tested our relationship more than the riot.

Toph woke at dawn because students practiced below us.

Aang kept leaving robes on the one chair.

Katara developed a hatred of the tiny stove.

I discovered that having an office ten feet from a metalbending class was incompatible with concentration.

We survived.

Barely.

The new house did not look grand.

That was deliberate.

We could have accepted donor money. Aang refused. Toph could have asked her family. She refused louder. Katara had Water Tribe contacts willing to send materials. She accepted only at market price.

We paid for it ourselves and built slowly.

The foundation remained old stone, reinforced rather than replaced.

Toph designed shallow metal channels beneath the floors so vibrations traveled cleanly between rooms without turning the house into an echo chamber. Door thresholds stayed low. Furniture had fixed positions where possible because consistency made spatial memory easier, but nothing became sacred enough that Toph could not approve changes.

“Approve?” she said when I used that word.

“Consent to changes in a shared accessibility system.”

“Better.”

Aang got his roof.

Not merely access.

A whole rooftop garden with low railings, meditation space, glider storage, and a landing platform beyond the main structure so Appa would stop destroying gutters.

Appa still destroyed one gutter.

Principle, apparently.

Katara got water.

A roof cistern collected rain into a filtered storage tank. Channels ran to the kitchen, washroom, garden, and a small healing room near the front entrance so she could treat neighbors without turning the entire house into a clinic.

I got a separate office in the courtyard wing.

Two doors.

One from the house.

One from the street.

Public visitors could enter without crossing private rooms.

The inside door locked from my side.

Aang tested it exactly once.

He knocked.

I did not answer.

He left.

I nearly cried over a door.

Toph found that hilarious until she discovered her training room had an exterior entrance too.

Then she stood in it for ten minutes saying nothing.

I did not mention the expression on her face.

We had learned.

The bedroom caused the most difficulty.

One bed?

Two?

Four?

Separate rooms plus shared room?

Toph insisted nobody was sleeping in a “relationship barracks.”

Katara wanted flexibility.

Aang wanted everyone to have private space.

I wanted to stop discussing beds with an architect who was taking notes.

We ended with four small personal rooms arranged around one larger shared sleeping room.

Not because we always slept separately.

Because love should not make solitude impossible.

Toph approved.

“Also if Twinkle Toes snores, I’m leaving.”

“I don’t snore.”

All three of us looked at him.

Aang looked betrayed.

The first night back, the house smelled like fresh wood, plaster, stone dust, and new beginnings that cost too much money.

We had almost no furniture in the common room because half our old pieces had not survived storage.

So we ate dinner on the floor.

Four bowls.

Again.

Katara looked around.

“It’s quiet.”

Toph tilted her head.

“No, it isn’t.”

She pointed.

“Cart two streets over. Somebody fixing a roof. Water in the east pipe. Aang bouncing his leg.”

Aang stopped.

Toph smiled.

“But it sounds right.”

That was better than quiet.

After dinner, Aang climbed to the roof.

Katara followed.

Toph pulled me toward the courtyard instead.

“What?”

She stood at the center where old foundation stone met the new reinforced ring.

“Stamp.”

I stared.

“Why?”

“Do it.”

I stamped one foot.

The vibration disappeared into the stone.

Toph shook her head.

“Again. Harder.”

I stamped.

She smiled.

“There.”

“What?”

“I can tell it’s you from anywhere in the house.”

My throat tightened.

“Toph—”

“Don’t.”

“Right.”

She hooked a finger through the cord holding the metal marker she had made me years—no, months—ago. Sometimes this life had become dense enough to feel longer than it was.

“If you need me,” she said, “drop this or stamp twice.”

“Okay.”

“If you don’t need me, don’t.”

“Okay.”

She kissed me quickly.

Then walked toward the roof stairs.

“Coming?”

We joined Aang and Katara above.

The city spread around us.

Cranes. Roofs. Smoke. New rail lines. Old walls. The cultural school on the hill. The river reflecting lantern light. The bridge rebuilt stronger than before.

Our home sat inside it, not above it.

Aang wrapped an arm around Katara.

Katara reached for Toph.

Toph leaned into me while pretending not to lean into anyone.

I looked down through the open roof hatch.

Four private rooms.

One shared room.

A public door.

A private door.

Ground beneath Toph’s feet.

Water within Katara’s reach.

Sky above Aang’s head.

A desk that could be closed behind me.

The house was not proof that we would stay forever.

That would have turned architecture into superstition.

It was proof that while we were here, we had learned how to make room for one another without making anyone disappear.

A house built for four.

Not four people forced into one shape.

The rebuilding took six weeks longer than promised.

This taught us that contractors in Cranefish Town were the most powerful force in the Four Nations because not even the Avatar could make one arrive on schedule.

“I could fix the wall,” Toph said for the ninth time.

“You are not rewiring the lamps,” Katara replied.

“I know metal.”

“You do not know electricity.”

“Electricity is just angry fire in a wire.”

Aang looked fascinated.

“No,” I said to both of them.

We learned the house through decisions.

Toph chose textured markers in the floor so she could identify room transitions instantly beneath her feet. Aang insisted on windows that opened wide enough to make every curtain dangerous. Katara designed storage at reachable heights instead of assuming all useful things belonged above someone’s head. I claimed a small room with a door and enough shelves for work that could be abandoned at the end of the day.

Nobody called it my retreat or sanctuary.

It was my office.

That mattered.

When the kitchen was finally finished, we stood in it without speaking.

Four work spaces. Wide paths. A table that did not wobble. Hooks where people actually needed them. Nothing grand.

Toph stamped once on the floor.

“Good.”

From her, this carried the weight of an architectural award.

Aang opened every window.

Katara immediately closed two because the papers were blowing away.

I leaned against the counter and listened to them argue.

The house sounded alive again.

Not finished.

Ours.

The first night back in the finished house, nobody slept well.

The walls sounded different. The windows caught the wind differently. Toph walked the rooms twice, mapping every altered seam through her feet. Aang kept opening doors just to see where they led, as if six weeks of construction had somehow changed the floor plan into a labyrinth.

Katara found me in the kitchen at midnight.

“Feels strange,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Good strange?”

“Ask me tomorrow.”

She smiled.

By morning, Toph had left shoes in the wrong place, Aang had forgotten a cup on the windowsill, and Katara had hung a towel over the chair she had specifically designated towel-free.

The house became familiar the moment we started inconveniencing one another in it again.

By the end of the week, the new house had acquired scratches, muddy footprints, one dent from Toph, and a scorch mark Aang refused to explain.

Katara stared at the damage.

“Now it looks lived in,” I offered.

She sighed.

Then she smiled.

Home had arrived before perfection did.

By then, lived-in was exactly what we wanted.
